newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Robinson seen facing tough task as UN rights boss.
newsitem.headline: Robinson seen facing tough task as UN rights boss.

text.p: Diplomats at the Geneva headquarters of the U.N. Center for Human Rights have welcomed the appointment of Irish President Mary Robinson as its chief, saying her high-profile image will help the institution's cause.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who pledged in an inaugural message last March to be a "champion for human rights", has taken a positive step to fulfil his promise with her appointment, according to diplomats, activists and U.N. sources.
As U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, Robinson will be expected to denounce repressive regimes while trying to get a foothold into countries where U.N. monitoring is needed.

The Human Rights Center employs 150 people in Geneva and deploys 250 observers in 12 field offices. They include 80 in Rwanda, its largest programme which has been severely curtailed since five members were gunned down last February.
Major rights groups including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have already endorsed Annan's choice, which must be endorsed by the General Assembly.
The International Commission of Jurists said of former member Robinson: "The ICJ believes the choice that has been made will greatly contribute to the cause of justice around the world."
But the lawyer and rights expert will have to do a fine balancing act if she is to avoid angering sensitive states in Asia, Africa and Latin America and disappointing Western ones.

"The Secretary-General has made perfectly clear that human rights is very important," Peter Van Wulfften Palthe, a Dutch diplomat respected for his negotiating skills in 1994 as chairman of the U.N. Human Rights Commission.
"We will have a high-profile kind of person dealing with rights in the United Nations. It is about time," he added.
But Palthe said: "She has to do a careful balancing act. On one hand she will be expected to be more active and on the other she cannot undermine acceptance of her office."
As a barrister she has pleaded landmark rights cases before European tribunals.
Annan has said he asked Robinson to step down from the Irish presidency by September so she could begin the U.N. job at the beginning of the General Assembly session.
David Weissbrodt, a U.S. member of the U.N. Sub-Commission on Human Rights, said: "Her political visibility before taking the post will assist her in being a visible High Commissioner.
"It is likely that she will take the post and move in the direction it needs to go -- a more active approach that was the promise of the High Commissioner in the first place," he added.

Jose Ayala Lasso, the first Human Rights Commissioner, took up the post in 1994 and left last March to become Ecuador's Foreign Minister amid criticism of his "quiet diplomacy" approach to the U.N. job.

Annan has yet to name a deputy to Robinson. Issa Diallo, a Senegalese in charge of U.N. conference services in Geneva, and Bertie Ramcharan, a long-time political adviser at the U.N. Human Rights Center who holds Guyanan nationality, are tipped as possible contenders.
"I am thrilled about Robinson. The big question now is whom will she bring as deputy," said one U.N. source.
Funding of the Center's activities, which comes from the U.N. regular budget, amounts to $24 million a year. Voluntary contributions double that.
